title: Chapter 2 — Origin Of The Anglo-Americans
paragraphs: Origin of the Anglo-Americans, and Its Importance in Relation to Their Future Condition.

After a human being is born, the early years pass obscurely in the labors or pleasures of childhood. As he grows up, the world receives him when manhood begins, and he comes into contact with other people. Only then is he studied for the first time, and people imagine that the seeds of the vices and virtues of his mature years are formed at that point. This, if I am not mistaken, is a great error. We must begin earlier. We must watch the infant in its mother’s arms; we must see the first images that the outside world casts upon the dark mirror of his mind and the first events he witnesses; we must hear the first words that awaken the sleeping powers of thought, and stand by his earliest efforts, if we want to understand the prejudices, habits, and passions that will rule his life. The whole man, so to speak, can be seen in the cradle of the child.

The growth of nations is something like this. They all bear some marks of their origin, and the circumstances that accompanied their birth and helped them rise affect their whole existence. If we could go back to the beginnings of states and examine the oldest records of their history, I do not doubt that we would find the first cause of their prejudices, habits, and ruling passions, in short, of everything that makes up what is called the national character. We would then find the explanation of certain customs that now seem at odds with the prevailing mores, of laws that conflict with established principles, and of the incoherent opinions found here and there in society, like those fragments of broken chains that we sometimes see hanging from the vault of a building and supporting nothing. This might explain the destinies of certain nations, which seem carried along by an unknown force toward ends of which they themselves are ignorant. But until now, facts have been lacking for research of this kind. The spirit of inquiry has come upon societies only in their later days, and when they finally looked back at their origin, time had already obscured it, or ignorance and pride had dressed it up in fables that hide the truth.

America is the only country where it has been possible to watch the natural and peaceful growth of a society, and where the influence of a state’s origin on its future condition can be clearly seen. When the peoples of Europe landed in the New World, their national characters were already fully formed. Each had a distinct face of its own. And since they had already reached the stage of civilization at which people come to study themselves, they have handed down to us a faithful picture of their opinions, their customs, and their laws. The men of the sixteenth century are almost as well known to us as our contemporaries. America therefore shows in broad daylight what the ignorance or rudeness of earlier ages hides from our research. We live near enough to the founding of the American states to know their elements accurately, and far enough from it to judge some of their results. So the men of our day seem destined to see further into the sequence of human events than their predecessors. Providence has given us a torch that our forefathers did not have, and has allowed us to discern fundamental causes in the history of the world that the obscurity of the past hid from them. If we carefully examine the social and political state of America after studying its history, we will be fully convinced that there is not an opinion, a custom, or a law, and I may even say not an event, on record that the origin of that people will not explain. Readers of this book will find the seed of everything that follows in this chapter, and the key to almost the whole work.

The emigrants who came at different times to settle the territory now covered by the American Union differed from each other in many respects. Their aims were not the same, and they governed themselves on different principles. Yet these men had certain features in common, and they were all in a similar situation. The tie of language is perhaps the strongest and most lasting that can unite human beings. All the emigrants spoke the same tongue, and all were offshoots of the same people. They were born in a country that had been shaken for centuries by the struggles of faction, in which every party had been obliged in its turn to place itself under the protection of the laws. Their political education had been completed in this rough school, and they were more familiar with the ideas of right and the principles of true freedom than most of their European contemporaries. At the time of their first emigrations, the parish system, that fruitful seed of free institutions, was deeply rooted in the habits of the English, and with it the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people had been brought into the heart of the monarchy of the House of Tudor.

The religious quarrels that have agitated the Christian world were then at their height. England had plunged into the new order of things with headlong force. The character of its people, which had always been sedate and thoughtful, became argumentative and austere. Intellectual debate had increased general knowledge, and the mind had received deeper cultivation. While religion was the topic of discussion, the morals of the people were reformed. All these national features can be recognized, more or less, in the character of those adventurers who came to seek a new home on the opposite shores of the Atlantic.

Another remark, to which we will return later, applies not only to the English but to the French, the Spaniards, and all the Europeans who successively settled in the New World. All these European colonies contained the elements, if not the full development, of a complete democracy. Two causes led to this result. It may safely be said that when the emigrants left the mother country, they generally had no idea of superiority over one another. The happy and the powerful do not go into exile, and there are no surer guarantees of equality among men than poverty and misfortune. On several occasions, however, persons of rank were driven to America by political and religious quarrels. Laws were made to set up a gradation of ranks, but it was soon found that the soil of America was opposed to a territorial aristocracy. To bring that stubborn land into cultivation, the constant effort of the owner himself, working for his own interest, was necessary. And once the ground was prepared, its produce proved insufficient to enrich a master and a farmer at the same time. The land was therefore naturally broken up into small portions, which the owner cultivated for himself. Land is the basis of an aristocracy, which clings to the soil that supports it. For an aristocracy is constituted not by privileges alone, nor by birth, but by landed property handed down from generation to generation. A nation may have immense fortunes and extreme wretchedness, but unless those fortunes are in land there is no aristocracy, only the class of the rich and the class of the poor.

At the time of their settlement, then, all the British colonies were very much alike. From their first beginnings, all of them seemed destined to see the growth, not of the aristocratic liberty of their mother country, but of the freedom of the middle and lower orders, of which the history of the world had so far furnished no complete example.

Within this general uniformity, however, several striking differences could be seen, and they need to be pointed out. Two branches can be distinguished in the Anglo-American family. Until now they have grown up without entirely mingling: one in the South, the other in the North.

Virginia received the first English colony; the emigrants took possession of it in 1607. The idea that mines of gold and silver are the sources of national wealth was at that time remarkably widespread in Europe. It was a fatal delusion, which has done more to impoverish the nations that adopted it, and has cost more lives in America, than war and bad laws combined. The men sent to Virginia *a were seekers of gold, adventurers without resources and without character, whose turbulent and restless spirit endangered the infant colony *b and made its progress uncertain. The artisans and farmers arrived afterward. Although they were a more moral and orderly sort of people, they were in no way above the level of the lower classes in England. *c No lofty conceptions, no intellectual system, guided the founding of these new settlements. The colony was scarcely established when slavery was introduced, *d and this was the main circumstance that has had such an enormous influence on the character, the laws, and all the future prospects of the South. Slavery, as we will show later, dishonors labor. It brings idleness into society, and with idleness come ignorance and pride, luxury and distress. It weakens the powers of the mind and numbs human activity. The influence of slavery, combined with the English character, explains the customs and social condition of the Southern States.

a [ The charter granted by the Crown of England in 1609 stipulated, among other conditions, that the adventurers should pay to the Crown a fifth of the produce of all gold and silver mines. See Marshall’s “Life of Washington,” vol. i. pp. 18-66.] [Footnote b: Stith (“History of Virginia”) says that a large portion of the adventurers were unprincipled young men from good families, whom their parents were glad to send away, along with dismissed servants, fraudulent bankrupts, and debauchees. Other men of the same kind, more inclined to plunder and destroy than to help the settlement, became the seditious leaders, and they easily drew this band into every sort of extravagance and excess. For the history of Virginia, see the following works:—
“History of Virginia, from the First Settlements in the year 1624,” by Smith.
“History of Virginia,” by William Stith.
“History of Virginia, from the Earliest Period,” by Beverley.]
c [ It was not until some time later that a certain number of rich English capitalists came to settle in the colony.]
d [ Slavery was introduced about the year 1620 by a Dutch ship that landed twenty Black people on the banks of the James River. See Chalmer.]

In the North, the same English foundation took on very different shades of character, and here I hope I may be allowed to go into some detail. The two or three central ideas on which the social theory of the United States rests first came together in the English colonies of the North, which are usually called the States of New England. *e At first the principles of New England reached only the neighboring states. They then moved on, one after another, to the more distant ones, and in the end they permeated the whole Confederation. Today their influence reaches beyond its borders, across the whole American world. The civilization of New England has been like a beacon lit on a hill: it first spreads its warmth all around, and then its glow colors the far horizon.
e [ The States of New England are the ones lying east of the Hudson. There are six of them today: 1, Connecticut; 2, Rhode Island; 3, Massachusetts; 4, Vermont; 5, New Hampshire; 6, Maine.]

The founding of New England was a new kind of spectacle, and all the circumstances attending it were unusual and original. The large majority of colonies were first settled either by men without education and without resources, driven from the land of their birth by poverty and misconduct, or by speculators and adventurers greedy for gain. Some settlements cannot even claim so honorable an origin. St. Domingo was founded by buccaneers, and the criminal courts of England originally supplied the population of Australia.

The settlers who established themselves on the shores of New England all belonged to the more independent classes of their native country. When they came together on American soil, they at once presented the unusual phenomenon of a society containing neither lords nor common people, neither rich nor poor. In proportion to their number, these men possessed a greater mass of intelligence than is found in any European nation of our own time. All of them, without a single exception, had received a good education, and many were known in Europe for their talents and their accomplishments. The other colonies had been founded by adventurers without families. The emigrants of New England brought with them the best elements of order and morality, and they landed in the wilderness accompanied by their wives and children. But what most especially distinguished them was the aim of their undertaking. Necessity had not forced them to leave their country; the social position they gave up was one to be regretted, and their means of living were secure. Nor did they cross the Atlantic to improve their situation or increase their wealth. The call that summoned them from the comforts of their homes was purely intellectual, and in facing the unavoidable sufferings of exile, their object was the triumph of an idea.

The emigrants, who rightly called themselves the Pilgrims, belonged to the English sect that had earned the name of Puritans through the austerity of its principles. Puritanism was more than a religious doctrine. On many points it coincided with the most absolute democratic and republican theories, and it was this tendency that had stirred up its most dangerous enemies. The government of the mother country persecuted the Puritans, and the habits of a society that rejected the rigor of their principles disgusted them. So they went off in search of some rude and unvisited corner of the world where they could live by their own opinions and worship God in freedom.

A few quotations will throw more light on the spirit of these pious adventurers than anything we could say about them. Nathaniel Morton, *f the historian of the first years of the settlement, opens his subject this way:
f [ “New England’s Memorial,” p. 13; Boston, 1826. See also “Hutchinson’s History,” vol. ii. p. 440.]

“Gentle Reader,—I have for some length of time looked upon it as a duty incumbent, especially on the immediate successors of those that have had so large experience of those many memorable and signal demonstrations of God’s goodness, viz., the first beginners of this Plantation in New England, to commit to writing his gracious dispensations on that behalf; having so many inducements thereunto, not onely otherwise but so plentifully in the Sacred Scriptures: that so, what we have seen, and what our fathers have told us (Psalm lxxviii. 3, 4), we may not hide from our children, showing to the generations to come the praises of the Lord; that especially the seed of Abraham his servant, and the children of Jacob his chosen (Psalm cv. 5, 6), may remember his marvelous works in the beginning and progress of the planting of New England, his wonders and the judgments of his mouth; how that God brought a vine into this wilderness; that he cast out the heathen, and planted it; that he made room for it and caused it to take deep root; and it filled the land (Psalm lxxx. 8, 9). And not onely so, but also that he hath guided his people by his strength to his holy habitation and planted them in the mountain of his inheritance in respect of precious Gospel enjoyments: and that as especially God may have the glory of all unto whom it is most due; so also some rays of glory may reach the names of those blessed Saints that were the main instruments and the beginning of this happy enterprise.”

It is impossible to read this opening paragraph without an involuntary feeling of religious awe. It breathes the very savor of the Gospel age. The author’s sincerity heightens the power of his language. The band that in his eyes was a mere party of adventurers gone out to seek their fortune overseas appears to the reader as the seed of a great nation, carried by Providence to a predestined shore.
The author then continues his account of the departure of the first pilgrims:—

“So they left that goodly and pleasant city of Leyden, *g which had been their resting-place for above eleven years; but they knew that they were pilgrims and strangers here below, and looked not much on these things, but lifted up their eyes to Heaven, their dearest country, where God hath prepared for them a city (Heb. xi. 16), and therein quieted their spirits. When they came to Delfs-Haven they found the ship and all things ready; and such of their friends as could not come with them followed after them, and sundry came from Amsterdam to see them shipt, and to take their leaves of them. One night was spent with little sleep with the most, but with friendly entertainment and Christian discourse, and other real expressions of true Christian love. The next day they went on board, and their friends with them, where truly doleful was the sight of that sad and mournful parting, to hear what sighs and sobs and prayers did sound among them; what tears did gush from every eye, and pithy speeches pierced each other’s heart, that sundry of the Dutch strangers that stood on the Key as spectators could not refrain from tears. But the tide (which stays for no man) calling them away, that were thus loth to depart, their Reverend Pastor falling down on his knees, and they all with him, with watery cheeks commended them with most fervent prayers unto the Lord and his blessing; and then, with mutual embraces and many tears they took their leaves one of another, which proved to be the last leave to many of them.”

g [ Most of the emigrants were devout Christians from the North of England. They had left their native country because they were “studious of reformation, and entered into covenant to walk with one another according to the primitive pattern of the Word of God.” They went to Holland and settled in the city of Leyden in 1610, where they lived for many years and were warmly respected by the Dutch. They left in 1620 for several reasons. The last was a fear that within a few generations their descendants would become Dutch and so lose their stake in the English nation. They preferred to extend His Majesty’s dominions and to live under their natural prince.—Translator’s Note.]

The emigrants numbered about 150, including the women and children. Their object was to plant a colony on the shores of the Hudson. But after being driven about for some time in the Atlantic Ocean, they were forced to land on that arid coast of New England which is now the site of the town of Plymouth. The rock on which the pilgrims disembarked is still shown. *h

h [ This rock has become an object of veneration in the United States. I have seen bits of it carefully preserved in several towns of the Union. Does this not show clearly enough how entirely all human power and greatness is in the soul of man? Here is a stone that the feet of a few outcasts pressed for an instant, and this stone becomes famous. A great nation treasures it, and its very dust is shared as a relic. And what has become of the gateways of a thousand palaces?]

“But before we pass on,” continues our historian, “let the reader with me make a pause and seriously consider this poor people’s present condition, the more to be raised up to admiration of God’s goodness towards them in their preservation: for being now passed the vast ocean, and a sea of troubles before them in expectation, they had now no friends to welcome them, no inns to entertain or refresh them, no houses, or much less towns to repair unto to seek for succor: and for the season it was winter, and they that know the winters of the country know them to be sharp and violent, subject to cruel and fierce storms, dangerous to travel to known places, much more to search unknown coasts. Besides, what could they see but a hideous and desolate wilderness, full of wilde beasts, and wilde men? and what multitudes of them there were, they then knew not: for which way soever they turned their eyes (save upward to Heaven) they could have but little solace or content in respect of any outward object; for summer being ended, all things stand in appearance with a weather-beaten face, and the whole country full of woods and thickets, represented a wild and savage hew; if they looked behind them, there was the mighty ocean which they had passed, and was now as a main bar or gulph to separate them from all the civil parts of the world.”

One should not suppose that Puritan piety was purely a matter of theory, or that it paid no attention to the course of worldly affairs. As I have already said, Puritanism was almost as much a political doctrine as a religious one. The emigrants had barely set foot on the barren coast that Nathaniel Morton describes when their first concern was to found a society. They did so by passing the following Act:

“In the name of God. Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, etc., etc., Having undertaken for the glory of God, and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the honor of our King and country, a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern parts of Virginia; Do by these presents solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politick, for our better ordering and preservation, and furtherance of the ends aforesaid: and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute and frame such just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, and officers, from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony: unto which we promise all due submission and obedience,” etc. *i

i [ The emigrants who founded the State of Rhode Island in 1638, those who landed at New Haven in 1637, the first settlers of Connecticut in 1639, and the founders of Providence in 1640 all started in the same way: they drew up a social contract, which every party concerned accepted. See “Pitkin’s History,” pp. 42 and 47.]

This happened in 1620, and from then on the emigration continued. The religious and political passions that ravaged the British Empire during the whole reign of Charles I drove fresh crowds of sectarians to the shores of America every year. In England the stronghold of Puritanism was in the middle classes, and the majority of the emigrants came from the middle classes. The population of New England grew rapidly. While the hierarchy of rank despotically classified the inhabitants of the mother country, the colony continued to present the new spectacle of a community uniform in all its parts. A democracy more perfect than any that antiquity had dreamed of sprang up, full-grown and fully armed, from the midst of an ancient feudal society.

The English government was not displeased with an emigration that removed the seeds of fresh discord and further revolutions. On the contrary, everything was done to encourage it, and great efforts were made to ease the hardships of those who sought shelter on American soil from the rigor of their own country’s laws. It seemed as if New England was a region given over to the dreams of fancy and the unrestrained experiments of innovators.

The English colonies have always had more freedom in their internal affairs, and more political independence, than the colonies of other nations, and this is one of the main causes of their prosperity. Yet the principle of liberty was nowhere carried further than in the States of New England.

It was generally accepted at that time that the territories of the New World belonged to whichever European nation first discovered them. Nearly the whole coast of North America thus became a British possession toward the end of the sixteenth century. The English government used several means to populate these new domains. Sometimes the King appointed a governor of his own choice, who ruled a portion of the New World in the name of the Crown and under its direct orders; *j this is the colonial system adopted by other countries of Europe. Sometimes the Crown granted certain tracts to an individual or to a company, *k in which case all civil and political power fell into the hands of one or more persons, who sold the lands and governed the inhabitants under the Crown’s inspection and control. Finally, a third system consisted in allowing a certain number of emigrants to form a political society under the protection of the mother country, and to govern themselves in everything not contrary to her laws. This mode of colonization, so remarkably favorable to liberty, was adopted only in New England. *l
j [ This was the case in the State of New York.]
k [ Maryland, the Carolinas, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey were in this situation. See “Pitkin’s History,” vol. i. pp. 11-31.]

l [ See the work entitled “Historical Collection of State Papers and other authentic Documents intended as materials for a History of the United States of America, by Ebenezer Hasard. Philadelphia, 1792,” for a large number of documents on the beginnings of the colonies, which are valuable both for what they say and for their authenticity. They include the various charters granted by the King of England and the first acts of the local governments.

See also the analysis of all these charters by Mr. Story, Judge of the Supreme Court of the United States, in the Introduction to his “Commentary on the Constitution of the United States.” It follows from these documents that the principles of representative government and the outward forms of political liberty were brought into all the colonies at their founding. The North put these principles into practice more fully than the South, but they were present everywhere.]

In 1628 *m Charles I gave a charter of this kind to the emigrants who set out to form the colony of Massachusetts. In general, though, the colonies of New England received charters only after they were already established. Plymouth, Providence, New Haven, the State of Connecticut, and the State of Rhode Island *n were founded without any help from the mother country and almost without her knowledge. The new settlers did not get their legal existence from the seat of the empire, although they did not deny its supremacy. They formed a society on their own initiative. Only thirty or forty years later, under Charles II, did a royal charter give their existence legal recognition.
m [ See “Pitkin’s History,” p, 35. See the “History of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay,” by Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 9.] [Footnote n: See “Pitkin’s History,” pp. 42, 47.]

This often makes it difficult, in studying the earliest historical and legislative records of New England, to detect the link that connected the emigrants with the land of their forefathers. They exercised the rights of sovereignty. They named their magistrates, made peace or declared war, issued police regulations, and enacted laws as if their allegiance were owed only to God. *o Nothing could be more curious, and at the same time more instructive, than the legislation of that period. It is there that the solution of the great social problem the United States now presents to the world is to be found.

o [ The people of Massachusetts had broken away from the forms kept in English criminal and civil procedure. As late as 1650, judicial decrees were still not issued under the royal title. See Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 452.]

Among these documents, one that stands out as especially characteristic is the code of laws that the little State of Connecticut issued in 1650. *p Its legislators *q start with the penal laws, and, strangely, they take their provisions straight from the text of Holy Scripture. “Whosoever shall worship any other God than the Lord,” says the preamble of the Code, “shall surely be put to death.” Ten or twelve provisions of the same kind follow, copied word for word from the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy. Blasphemy, sorcery, adultery, *r and rape carried the death penalty, and a son who outraged his parents was to pay for it in the same way. The legislation of a rude and half-civilized people was being applied to an educated and moral community. As a result, the death penalty was written into the statute book more often than ever before, yet it was enforced against the guilty more rarely than ever.
p [ Code of 1650, p. 28; Hartford, 1830.]

q [ See also “Hutchinson’s History,” vol. i. pp. 435, 456, for the analysis of the penal code that the Colony of Massachusetts adopted in 1648. It is built on the same principles as the code of Connecticut.]

r [ Massachusetts law also made adultery punishable by death, and Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 441, says that several people were in fact executed for it. He tells a curious story from the year 1663. A married woman had had an adulterous relationship with a young man. Her husband died, and she married her lover. Several years went by before people began to suspect the couple’s earlier adulterous relationship. They were thrown into prison and brought to trial, and they very narrowly escaped the death penalty.]

In this body of penal laws, the legislators cared above all about keeping the community orderly and moral. They invaded the realm of conscience again and again, and there was hardly a sin that the magistrates could not censure. The reader has seen how rigorously these laws punished rape and adultery. Sex between unmarried people was also harshly suppressed. The judge had the power to impose a fine, a whipping, or marriage *s on offenders, and if the records of the old courts of New Haven can be believed, such prosecutions were not uncommon. One sentence, dated the first of May, 1660, fines and reprimands a young woman who was accused of using improper language and letting herself be kissed. *t The Code of 1650 is full of preventive measures. It deals severely with idleness and drunkenness. *u Innkeepers may not serve any customer more than a fixed amount of liquor, and plain lying, whenever it may do harm, *v is checked with a fine or a flogging. Elsewhere the legislator completely forgets the great principles of religious toleration that he himself had defended in Europe. He makes attendance at divine service compulsory, *w and he even goes so far as to inflict severe punishment, ** and even death, on Christians who chose to worship God according to a ritual different from his own. *x At times the zeal of his enactments leads him down to the pettiest details; the same Code, for instance, contains a law that forbids the use of tobacco. *y We must not forget that these fantastical and vexatious laws were not imposed from above. All the people concerned voted for them freely, and the customs of the community were even more austere and puritanical than the laws. In 1649 a solemn association was formed in Boston to put a stop to the worldly luxury of long hair. *z

s [ Code of 1650, p. 48. Judges seem sometimes to have combined these punishments, as in a sentence pronounced in 1643 (p. 114, “New Haven Antiquities”), in which Margaret Bedford, convicted of loose conduct, was sentenced to be whipped and then to marry her accomplice, Nicholas Jemmings.]
t [ “New Haven Antiquities,” p. 104. See also “Hutchinson’s History” for several equally extraordinary cases.]

* [ This was not peculiar to Connecticut. See, for instance, the law which, on September 13, 1644, banished the Anabaptists from the State of Massachusetts. (“Historical Collection of State Papers,” vol. i. p. 538.) See also the law against the Quakers, passed on October 14, 1656: “Whereas,” says the preamble, “an accursed race of heretics called Quakers has sprung up,” etc. The statute imposes a heavy fine on any ship captain who brings Quakers into the country. Quakers found in the colony are to be whipped and put to hard labor in prison. Members of the sect who defend their opinions are to be fined first, then imprisoned, and finally driven out of the province.—“Historical Collection of State Papers,” vol. i. p. 630.]
x [ Under the penal law of Massachusetts, a Catholic priest who had once been driven out of the colony and then set foot in it again could be put to death.]
y [ Code of 1650, p. 96.]
z [ “New England’s Memorial,” p. 316. See Appendix, E.]

These errors are no doubt discreditable to human reason. They attest the inferiority of our nature, which is incapable of taking firm hold of what is true and just, and is often reduced to a choice between two excesses. Closely connected with this penal legislation, which bears such striking marks of a narrow sectarian spirit and of religious passions warmed by persecution and still fermenting among the people, there is a body of political laws that, though written two hundred years ago, is still ahead of the liberties of our age. The general principles that are the groundwork of modern constitutions were imperfectly known in Europe in the seventeenth century, and not completely triumphant even in Great Britain. Yet the laws of New England recognized and established all of them: the intervention of the people in public affairs, the free voting of taxes, the responsibility of authorities, personal liberty, and trial by jury were all positively established without debate. From these fruitful principles, consequences have been drawn and applications made such as no nation in Europe has yet ventured to attempt.

In Connecticut the electoral body consisted, from its origin, of all the citizens. This is readily understood *a when we recall that this people enjoyed an almost perfect equality of fortune and a still greater uniformity of opinions. *b In Connecticut at this period all the executive officials were elected, including the Governor of the State. *c Citizens above the age of sixteen were obliged to bear arms. They formed a national militia, which appointed its own officers and was to hold itself ready at all times to march to the defense of the country. *d
a [ Constitution of 1638, p. 17.]

b [ In 1641 the General Assembly of Rhode Island declared unanimously that the government of the State was a democracy, and that power rested with the body of free citizens, who alone had the right to make the laws and to oversee their execution.—Code of 1650, p. 70.]
c [ “Pitkin’s History,” p. 47.]
d [ Constitution of 1638, p. 12.]

In the laws of Connecticut, as in all the laws of New England, we find the seed, and the gradual growth, of the independence of the township, which today is the life and mainspring of American liberty. Most European nations began their political life in the upper ranks of society, and it was passed down slowly and imperfectly to the other members of the social body. In America it was the other way around. One may say that the township was organized before the county, the county before the State, and the State before the Union. In New England, townships were fully and definitively established as early as 1650. Local interests, passions, rights, and duties gathered and clung around the independence of the township as around a nucleus. It made room for a truly political life, thoroughly democratic and republican. The colonies still acknowledged the supremacy of the mother country, and monarchy was still the law of the State, yet the republic was already alive in every township. The townships appointed their own magistrates of every kind, taxed themselves, and collected their own taxes. *e In the New England parish the principle of representation was not adopted. Instead, as at Athens, the affairs of the community were debated in the marketplace by a general assembly of the citizens.
e [ Code of 1650, p. 80.]

Anyone who studies the laws issued in this first era of the American republics cannot help being struck by how much they show of the science of government and how advanced their theory of legislation was. The ideas they express about the duties of society toward its members are clearly much loftier and broader than those of European lawmakers of the time. They imposed obligations that were neglected elsewhere. In the States of New England, the condition of the poor was provided for from the start. *f Strict measures were taken to maintain the roads, and surveyors were appointed to look after them. *g Registers were set up in every parish, in which the results of public deliberations and the births, deaths, and marriages of the citizens were recorded. *h Clerks were ordered to keep these registers. *i Officers were put in charge of administering unclaimed inheritances and of settling disputes over boundary marks. Many other officers were created whose chief task was to maintain public order in the community. *j The law takes up a thousand useful provisions for social needs that are, at present, very poorly felt in France. [Footnote f: Ibid., p. 78.]
h [ See “Hutchinson’s History,” vol. i. p. 455.]
i [ Code of 1650, p. 86.]

But it is in the attention it gives to public education that the original character of American civilization shows most clearly. “It being,” says the law, “one chief project of Satan to keep men from the knowledge of the Scripture by persuading from the use of tongues, to the end that learning may not be buried in the graves of our forefathers, in church and commonwealth, the Lord assisting our endeavors. . . .” *k What follows are clauses that establish schools in every township and require the inhabitants, under heavy fines, to support them. Schools of a higher kind were founded in the same way in the more populous districts. The municipal authorities had to see that parents sent their children to school. They were empowered to fine anyone who refused, and if the refusal continued, society took the parent’s place, took possession of the child, and deprived the father of the natural rights he was using so badly. The reader will surely have noticed the preamble of these enactments: in America, religion is the road to knowledge, and observing the divine laws leads a person to civil freedom.

Suppose we glance quickly at the state of American society in 1650 and then turn to the condition of Europe at the same time, especially the Continent. We cannot help being astonished. On the Continent at the beginning of the seventeenth century, absolute monarchy had triumphed everywhere over the ruins of the oligarchical and feudal liberties of the Middle Ages. Ideas of right were never more thoroughly confused than amid the splendor and literature of Europe. The people had never been less active in politics, and the principles of true freedom had never been less widely known. Yet at that very moment, those principles, scorned or unknown by the nations of Europe, were being proclaimed in the wilderness of the New World and accepted as the future creed of a great people. The boldest theories of human reason were being put into practice by a community so humble that not a single statesman bothered to notice it. A legislation without precedent was produced on the spot by the imagination of the citizens. In the heart of this obscure democracy, which had so far produced no generals, no philosophers, and no authors, a man could stand up before a free people and give the following fine definition of liberty. *l

l [ Mather’s “Magnalia Christi Americana,” vol. ii. p. 13. This speech was made by Winthrop. He had been accused of arbitrary actions during his time as magistrate, but after he made the speech of which the above is a fragment, he was acquitted by acclamation, and from then on he was always re-elected governor of the State. “Nor would I have you to mistake in the point of your own liberty. There is a liberty of a corrupt nature which is effected both by men and beasts to do what they list, and this liberty is inconsistent with authority, impatient of all restraint; by this liberty ‘sumus omnes deteriores’: ’tis the grand enemy of truth and peace, and all the ordinances of God are bent against it. But there is a civil, a moral, a federal liberty which is the proper end and object of authority; it is a liberty for that only which is just and good: for this liberty you are to stand with the hazard of your very lives and whatsoever crosses it is not authority, but a distemper thereof. This liberty is maintained in a way of subjection to authority; and the authority set over you will, in all administrations for your good, be quietly submitted unto by all but such as have a disposition to shake off the yoke and lose their true liberty, by their murmuring at the honor and power of authority.”

What I have said is enough to show Anglo-American civilization in its true light. It is the product of two distinct elements (and this should be kept constantly in mind). In other places these have often been in conflict, but in America they have been admirably joined and blended. I mean the spirit of Religion and the spirit of Liberty.

The settlers of New England were at once ardent sectarians and daring innovators. Some of their religious opinions were very narrow, but they were entirely free of political prejudices. Two tendencies followed from this. They were distinct but not opposed, and they can be constantly seen in the customs as well as in the laws of the country.

One might imagine that men who gave up their friends, their families, and their native land for a religious conviction would be wholly absorbed in the pursuit of the intellectual benefits they had paid for so dearly. Yet they strove just as energetically to gain wealth, moral enjoyment, and the comforts as well as the liberties of this world. That energy is hardly less than the energy with which they devoted themselves to Heaven.

Political principles and all human laws and institutions were shaped and changed at their pleasure. The barriers of the society they were born in fell before them, and the old principles that had governed the world for ages were gone. A path with no turning and a field with no horizon opened up to the eager, exploring curiosity of man. But at the boundary of the political world he stops his inquiries. He prudently sets aside the use of his most formidable faculties. He no longer agrees to doubt or to innovate. He carefully avoids lifting the curtain of the sanctuary, and he yields with submissive respect to truths that he will not discuss. So in the moral world everything is classified, adjusted, decided, and foreseen, while in the political world everything is stirred up, uncertain, and disputed. In the one there is a passive, though voluntary, obedience. In the other there is an independence that scorns experience and is jealous of authority.

These two tendencies seem very different, yet they are far from conflicting. They advance together and support each other. Religion sees that civil liberty gives the faculties of man a noble field of exercise, and that the political world is a field the Creator prepared for the efforts of the intelligence. Religion is content with the freedom and power it enjoys in its own sphere and with the place it holds. Its empire is never more securely established than when it reigns in the hearts of men with no support beyond its own native strength. Religion is no less the companion of liberty in all its battles and triumphs, the cradle of its infancy, and the divine source of its claims. Religion is the safeguard of morality, and morality is the best security of law and the surest pledge of freedom. *m

Reasons of Certain Anomalies Which the Laws and Customs of the Anglo-Americans Present
Remains of aristocratic institutions in the midst of a complete democracy — Why? — Distinction to be carefully drawn between what is of Puritan origin and what is of English origin.

The reader is cautioned not to draw too general or too absolute a conclusion from what has been said. The social condition, the religion, and the customs of the first emigrants undoubtedly had an immense influence on the destiny of their new country. Nevertheless, they were not in a position to found a state of things that depended on them alone. No one can entirely shake off the influence of the past. The settlers, whether they meant to or not, mixed habits and ideas that came from their education and from the traditions of their country with the habits and ideas that were purely their own. To judge the Anglo-Americans of the present day, it is therefore necessary to distinguish what is of Puritan origin from what is of English origin.

Laws and customs are often found in the United States that contrast sharply with everything around them. These laws seem to have been drawn up in a spirit contrary to the general tenor of American legislation, and these customs are just as opposed to the tone of society. If the English colonies had been founded in an age of darkness, or if their origin had already been lost in the passage of years, the problem would be unsolvable.

I shall give a single example to illustrate my point. American civil and criminal procedure has only two means of action, committal and bail. The magistrate’s first step is to require security from the defendant, or to put him in prison if he refuses. Only then are the grounds of the accusation and the seriousness of the charges against him discussed. It is evident that legislation of this kind is hostile to the poor man and favors only the rich. The poor man cannot always produce security, even in a civil case, and if he has to wait for justice in prison, he is soon reduced to distress. The wealthy man, on the other hand, always escapes imprisonment in civil cases. More than that, he can easily avoid the punishment that awaits him for a crime by forfeiting his bail. So for him all the penalties of the law come down to fines. *n Nothing could be more aristocratic than this system of legislation. Yet in America it is the poor who make the law, and they usually keep the greatest social advantages for themselves. The explanation of this phenomenon is to be found in England. The laws I am speaking of are English, *o and the Americans have kept them, however repugnant they may be to the tenor of their legislation and to the mass of their ideas. After its habits, the thing a nation is least likely to change is its civil legislation. Civil laws are familiarly known only to lawyers, whose direct interest is to keep them as they are, good or bad, simply because they themselves are well versed in them. The body of the nation hardly knows them. It sees their action only in particular cases, has some difficulty grasping their tendency, and obeys them without thinking. I have given one instance where it would have been easy to cite a great many others. The surface of American society is, if I may put it this way, covered with a layer of democracy, and from underneath it the old aristocratic colors sometimes show through.
n [ Crimes no doubt exist for which bail is inadmissible, but they are few in number.]
